extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of history, literature, and leadership; creative writers studying heroic character and statesmanship
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for depicting and judging 'heroic' persons (especially leaders) — what qualities constitute greatness, how to read speeches/actions, and how to distinguish true greatness from showy or hypocritical behavior. Useful for creative writers, historians, and critics modeling heroic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic/visionary depth
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero can be 'the inarticulate Prophet' — rude, confused outwardly, yet possessing 'savage depth' and 'wild sincerity'; a man with his whole soul seeing and struggling to see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate inner vision rather than surface polish. Carlyle uses Cromwell and Samuel Johnson as examples: outward hypochondria, nervous dreams, or incoherent speech do not negate a clear internal meaning. Look for intensity of sympathy, insight, and an imperative to grasp 'the heart of things.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to act (Tugend) — courage and faculty to do
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue and hero-hood are primarily Tugend (doing): Courage and the faculty to _do_, not mere eloquence or formal virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying or judging a hero, emphasize practical capacity, resolute action, and the power to accomplish tasks. Intellectual or rhetorical elegance is secondary to demonstrable effectiveness and moral courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity through prayer and earnestness rather than polished eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero's devotion and sincerity are often expressed in prayer, rhapsodic preaching, or extempore utterance; 'warmth, depth, sincerity are all that is required.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value spontaneous, heartfelt expression (e.g., extempore prayer) over mechanized rhetorical skill. Use scenes of prayer, collective supplication, or anguished devotion to signal authentic motive and moral seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful speech need not be polished
rubrics_metrics.description: If words are true, they can be left to shift for themselves; speaking without premeditation can still carry weight — Cromwell's rough speeches were 'impressive' though not polished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't equate rough or fragmented rhetoric with incoherence of thought. In character-writing, allow inarticulate or abrupt speech to reveal conviction and force. Avoid treating lack of polish as evidence of weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reticence and strategic secrecy (not necessarily hypocrisy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A superior man must have 'reticences' — he decides how much of his mind to show; leave the inquirer uninformed rather than misinformed. This discretion is often mistaken for dissimulation or hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish strategic reserve from moral falseness. A leader's withholding of full thoughts from every interlocutor can be prudent. In narratives, show selective disclosure as a protective and pragmatic trait, not automatically villainous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish kinds of ambition: noble duty vs vain self-seeking
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two ambitions: the blamable, prurient desire to shine; and the laudable, inevitable impulse to unfold one's nature and serve a higher purpose ('to unfold your _self_').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess motive and fitness for office: a character's drive to lead may be legitimate duty if matched by capacity and a public-minded purpose. Contrast selfish, attention-seeking ambition (anti-pattern) with duty-driven striving that serves others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence as a moral and creative virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Empire of Silence' — noble silent men who think and work without clamour are the 'salt of the Earth'; silence is higher than public display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use silence to signal depth. Characters who avoid public show, who keep thought inward, should be read as potentially great rather than merely passive. Avoid equating publicity with virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a single decisive chief
rubrics_metrics.description: In movements and crises, a single Chief or King is often indispensable; many zealous men without a leader are powerless against one decisive man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting collective action, represent the decisive leader as pivotal: narrative weight should be given to the presence or absence of a commanding personality (example: Montrose's victories vs leaderless Puritans). This criterion values decisive individuality in political drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reality over constitutional/formal formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'Reality' is at hand, abstract constitutional formulas and pedantries can be obstacles; Carlyle defends acts like Cromwell's dismissal of Parliament as appeals to practicable fact over mere legalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In character and plot choices, prioritize plausible practical responses to crises over adherence to formalities. Show tension between abstract principles and exigent realities; expose pedantry as potentially destructive when action is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting career goal for lived course (no hindsight-programming)
rubrics_metrics.description: It's an error to treat a great man's life as if perfectly premeditated; careers are an 'unwound skein of possibilities' rather than a mapped drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write lives/biographies avoiding teleological narration that projects later aims backward. Portray contingency, gradual formation, and partial ignorance rather than omniscient planning. Historiographic anti-pattern: assuming the end was intended from the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical 'fanatic→hypocrite' theory inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: The common theory that sincere fanatics inevitably become hypocrites (Hume's view) is oversimplified; true-natured heroes retain core sincerity despite faults and falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging character arcs, allow for complexity: lapses and insincerities may occur, but do not automatically erase a lifetime of earnest motive. Use metaphors (Antaeus regaining strength from earth) to show resilience of true character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge greatness by inner purpose and moral seriousness, not by public notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men are not sustained by public applause; Cromwell and Johnson were already 'there'—Death, Judgment and Eternity formed the background of their thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters by their internal moral framework and seriousness about ultimate matters rather than by their desire for fame. Show inner reckonings, spiritual background, and refusal of spectacle as marks of authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to accept heavy ambiguous responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: True leaders accept burden and ambiguous responsibility when institutions fail (Cromwell accepting Protectorship because otherwise Anarchy would follow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict moments of agonized choice and acceptance of onerous duty as central to heroic stature. The willingness to assume unpopular authority for the sake of preventing ruin is a test of greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final penitential sincerity as evidence of integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero's end—broken prayers, concern for judgment—can serve as proof of ongoing sincerity; Cromwell's last words are taken as evidence against calling him a hypocrite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narrative arcs, final scenes of confession, prayer, or moral reckoning can retroactively validate a character's sincerity. Use closing moments of contrition or appeal to a higher judge to complicate moral verdicts.
